section_summary: This section documents Japan’s expanding military mobilization during the Sino-Japanese War, especially troop embarkations through Kobe, Osaka, Hiroshima, and nearby ports, together with reports on force strength, strategy, discipline, and Japanese public opinion. Later documents cover Imperial Headquarters, the National General Mobilization Law, military manpower, amnesties and punishments, alleged divisions within the army, and official War Office propaganda advocating prolonged war and total national mobilization. The reports also record restrictions on photography, concern over army misconduct in China, anti-British sentiment, and generally favorable attitudes toward the United States.

subfiles.title: Japan Chronicle warning against carrying cameras
subfiles.about: A newspaper excerpt warns foreigners that carrying cameras near guarded facilities in Kobe will provoke police or military scrutiny.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure comes from Scott's August 10 letter to the American Ambassador. It reports that foreigners should avoid possessing cameras through August 13, especially at the Iirume Boathouse, where officers were monitoring photography and other irregularities.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 154: Political and Military Matters in Kobe, Japan
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; enclosure addressed to Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.about: Scott reports troop embarkations from Kobe, additional divisional mobilizations, and local reactions to the expanding war in China.
subfiles.summary: Scott estimates that about 50,000 troops left Kobe between August 8 and 13 and reports that the 11th Division was preparing to embark from Shikoku for Shanghai while the 14th Division near Utsunomiya had mobilized. He describes subdued popular enthusiasm, business anxiety over taxes, continued orderly relations with foreigners and Chinese residents, and disruption surrounding the arrival of the Empress of Japan that was caused chiefly by quarantine rather than military requisitioning of trains.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 164: Political and Military Matters in Japan
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; enclosure addressed to Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.about: Scott describes renewed troop movements through Kobe and the Inland Sea during late August and early September.
subfiles.summary: Kobe's waterfront and customs compound were placed under military control while approximately a division, including cavalry, embarked during the first week of September. Travelers reported very heavy troopship traffic through Moji and the Shimonoseki Strait, while Scott also discusses government chartering of commercial vessels, possibly on renewable three-month terms.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 165: Political and Military Matters in Kobe, Japan
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; enclosure addressed to Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.about: Scott reports congestion caused by troop embarkations at Osaka and continuing military rail traffic through Kobe.
subfiles.summary: The Kobe harbor master attributed difficulty assigning a berth to the USS Gold Star to military congestion originating at Osaka. Scott states that eighteen troopships had sailed from Osaka, with more awaiting troops, while troop trains continued to pass through Kobe.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2607 concerning the Sino-Japanese conflict
subfiles.about: Grew forwards Scott's September 20 report on troop movements, Japanese military strength, and opinion in Kobe.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure identifies troops departing Osaka as the 9th Division from Asahikawa and reports that elements of the 1st Division, including artillery, cavalry, and transport units, were embarking at Kobe. Sources estimated 300,000 Japanese troops in China and another 600,000 under arms or immediately available, while Scott described worried business opinion, tighter port regulations, and continuing friendliness toward the United States.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 171: Military Matters in Kobe, Japan
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; enclosure addressed to Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.about: Scott independently transmits the September 20 report on troop embarkations, reserves, local morale, and port restrictions.
subfiles.summary: The report repeats the identification of the 9th Division from Asahikawa and elements of Tokyo's 1st Division moving through Osaka and Kobe. It also discusses estimates of Japanese manpower, the retention of stronger reserve classes in Japan, anxiety among businesspeople, camera restrictions at the port, and favorable views of American neutrality.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 174: Military Matters in Kobe, Japan
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; enclosure addressed to Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.about: Scott reports continuing embarkations from Kobe, rumors of fighting in Manchuria, and local attitudes toward America.
subfiles.summary: The balance of the Kanazawa Division and troops of the 8th Division from Hirosaki were reportedly embarking at Kobe, whose traffic had increased because cholera halted sailings from Hiroshima. Travelers from Dairen reported a possible mutiny and a train bombing north of Mukden, while ships arriving from Dairen carried soldiers' ashes that suggested fighting in Manchuria. Scott observed no reduction in friendly feeling toward the United States despite American criticism of the bombing of Nanking.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Telegram No. 510 on the Japanese Army
subfiles.about: The sheet directs readers to a telegram reporting Major Creswell's assessment of Japanese Army objectives and public attitudes.
subfiles.summary: The cross-reference identifies Telegram No. 510 from Japan. It describes the subject as the Japanese Army's objectives in the Sino-Japanese conflict and the Japanese public's attitude toward them.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 510: Major Creswell's report on Japanese strategy and opinion
subfiles.about: Grew transmits Major Creswell's analysis of the enlarged Kwantung Army, Japanese operations in China, and domestic political attitudes.
subfiles.summary: Creswell estimates the Kwantung Army and forces under its control at about 230,000 men, enlarged because of fears concerning the Soviet Union, Outer Mongolia, and disaffection in the Manchukuo Army. He argues that the Shanghai and North China campaigns were connected and that Japan might seek a decisive blow through Nanking while retaining ample manpower reserves. The report says Japanese society was firmly behind the armed services but increasingly questioned the Konoe Cabinet's coordination and leadership.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 179: Military Matters in Kobe, Japan
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; enclosure addressed to Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.about: Scott reports a temporary halt in Kobe troop embarkations and Japanese reactions to recent American statements.
subfiles.summary: Troop movements continued through October 8, including 2,500 men of the 2nd Division from Tsuruga and reservists aged roughly 25 to 38. With the Hiroshima cholera outbreak subsiding, Kobe's wharves reopened and embarkations paused, though Scott expected the lull to be temporary. He found resentment focused on Britain and little present hostility toward the United States.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Japanese military mobilization
subfiles.about: The sheet references a report on mobilizing Japan's effective military power and establishing special headquarters.
subfiles.summary: The cross-reference points to another file concerning military affairs. Its synopsis says Japan was mobilizing effective military power and planning several special headquarters to place the country on the strongest possible footing.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on anti-British sentiment in Japan
subfiles.to: Sumner Welles and the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The memorandum highlights Scott's account of extreme anti-British remarks by prominent Japanese businessmen.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum calls attention to the last two paragraphs of an attached Kobe report describing rabid anti-British sentiment. At an Osaka Fog Club dinner, prominent Japanese industrialists allegedly boasted that Japan could seize Hong Kong, other British possessions, Canada, and the Philippine Islands without effective British resistance.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 184: Military Matters in Kobe, Japan
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; enclosure addressed to Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.about: Scott discusses reduced troop movements at Kobe, naval-visit restrictions, and sharply anti-British attitudes among Japanese business leaders.
subfiles.summary: Scott reports that most troop embarkations had shifted to the screened port of Ujina near Hiroshima, with lesser activity at Osaka, leaving Kobe harbor relatively uncrowded despite Japanese objections to further foreign naval visits. Japanese contacts continued to discount American criticism while directing hostility toward Britain. A British resident's account of a Fog Club dinner illustrated belligerent claims that Japan could seize British and American-associated possessions.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Telegram No. 562 on Imperial Headquarters
subfiles.about: The sheet references a telegram on the creation, organization, and functions of Japanese Imperial Headquarters.
subfiles.summary: The cross-reference identifies Telegram No. 562 and summarizes the official November 20 statement establishing Imperial Headquarters. It also notes an assessment of the likelihood of a formal declaration of war.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 562: Establishment of Imperial Headquarters
subfiles.about: Grew reports the official organization and functions of Japan's newly established Imperial Headquarters.
subfiles.summary: Imperial Headquarters was defined as the Emperor's instrument for supreme command, strategic planning, and army-navy coordination, without merging the military command with the government. Cabinet members would not belong to it but could be invited to conferences. The Embassy continued to believe that foreign arms and ammunition reaching China would be decisive in determining whether Japan formally declared war.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 191: Military Matters in Kobe, Japan
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; enclosure addressed to Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.about: Scott reports the departure of approximately 10,000 second reservists from Kobe.
subfiles.summary: After a lull, about 10,000 soldiers concentrated in Kobe during the preceding four or five days. They were second reservists aged approximately 27 to 35, drawn from divisions based at Tokyo, Sendai, and Nagoya and including infantry, artillery, and transport units.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Japanese Imperial Headquarters
subfiles.about: The sheet references a despatch discussing Imperial Headquarters and enclosing the 1903 ordinance governing it.
subfiles.summary: The note points to Despatch No. 2657 concerning the establishment of Japanese Imperial Headquarters. It records that the despatch enclosed a translation of Ordinance No. 293 of December 28, 1903.

subfiles.title: Letter reporting large troop movements through Kobe
subfiles.about: Scott reports the departure of roughly 60,000 troops, further arrivals at Kobe, and continuing business pessimism.
subfiles.summary: Scott states that the exodus of approximately 60,000 mixed troops had been completed and that another estimated 20,000 young soldiers, including regiments of the 14th Division, were arriving. Billeted officers and soldiers claimed that about one million Japanese troops were already in China. Although local efforts sought better British-Japanese relations and hostility toward Americans had not increased, pessimism persisted among Japanese professionals and businesspeople.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Telegram No. 1195 on divisions within the Japanese Army
subfiles.about: The sheet references a Shanghai telegram about conflict between senior and junior Japanese Army officers.
subfiles.summary: The note summarizes a report by New York Times correspondent Abend on a struggle between senior officers led by Matsui and junior officers including Colonel Hashimoto. It connects Hashimoto's forces with the attack on the USS Panay and says Matsui's headquarters wanted the account published in America and then recabled to Japan.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1195: Reported struggle within the Japanese Army
subfiles.about: Gauss reports confidential information supplied to Hallett Abend concerning a struggle between Japanese senior and junior officers.
subfiles.summary: Abend said Matsui's headquarters had flown him material alleging conflict between senior officers and junior officers such as Colonel Hashimoto, whose Wuhu forces were linked to the USS Panay attack. The headquarters reportedly hoped publication in New York would allow the information to return to Japan because no Japanese newspaper would publish it independently.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on disciplining officers after attacks on foreign vessels
subfiles.about: The sheet references a report on disagreement in the Japanese command over disciplining officers responsible for attacks on American and British vessels.
subfiles.summary: The note cites commentary from the New York Times concerning a split in the Japanese command. It also records that the Department expected the findings of the United States Naval Court of Inquiry into the Panay incident within several days.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on discipline and the February 26 element in the Japanese Army
subfiles.about: The sheet references an Embassy assessment of whether radical February 26 elements could challenge constituted authority.
subfiles.summary: Major Creswell believed there was little likelihood of a revival of the February 26 element strong enough to strike at the government or seriously influence military operations. The Embassy reported no evidence contradicting that assessment.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Telegram No. 105 on national-resource mobilization
subfiles.about: The sheet references a telegram concerning a bill to place productive industry under wartime control.
subfiles.summary: The cross-reference describes the government's proposed national-resources mobilization bill. Its stated purpose was to place all forms of productive industry under the control of Imperial Headquarters during war.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 105: Proposed national-resources mobilization bill
subfiles.about: Grew evaluates political opposition to the government's proposed national-resources mobilization bill.
subfiles.summary: The National Planning Board and Bureau of Legislation were drafting a measure permitting government control over virtually all productive industry during war or an incident. Parliamentary critics objected to broad delegations of power and feared authoritarian government and increased army control. Grew nevertheless expected passage after revisions clarifying the bill's scope.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Matsui's reported replacement by Hata
subfiles.about: The sheet references naval communications reporting a change in Japanese Army command in China.
subfiles.summary: The note states that General Matsui was reportedly being relieved by General Hata. It points to Navy Department messages numbered 1618 through 1712.

subfiles.title: Memorandum and enclosure on the Imperial Precepts to Soldiers and Sailors
subfiles.doc_type: Department of State memorandum with reference extract
subfiles.about: The memorandum compares reported Japanese Army atrocities in China with the ethical standards of the Imperial Precepts.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum notes reports of unrestrained violence in occupied China and suggests invoking the Imperial Precepts when protesting Japanese military misconduct. The appended extract stresses loyalty, obedience, considerate treatment of inferiors, disciplined courage, gentleness, faithfulness, righteousness, and simplicity. The writer argues that reported acts in China were strikingly inconsistent with this code and with Japan's former reputation for military discipline.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 1212 on cancellation of army punishments
subfiles.about: The sheet references a Shanghai despatch concerning cancellation of a Japanese Army punishment order.
subfiles.summary: The note points to Despatch No. 1212 and an announcement made in Tokyo. Its subject is the cancellation of an Army order of punishment.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1212: Announcement in Tokyo of cancellation of Army order of punishment
subfiles.about: Gauss forwards a news report on an imperial amnesty and cancellation of certain Japanese Army punishments.
subfiles.summary: Gauss calls attention to an Army order canceling punishments for offenses committed before February 11, possibly including disciplinary infractions in China and offenses against Americans or the American flag. The enclosed Reuters report describes an Empire Day amnesty restoring rights to 300,000 people and reducing sentences imposed on participants in the 1936 army revolt and the 1932 naval-terrorist incident. It also describes mass celebrations in Tokyo and Japan's greatly enlarged 1938 budget.

subfiles.title: Report No. 9232: Recruitment—Enlisted personnel
subfiles.about: The report evaluates rumors that Japan planned to lower its conscription age and physical standards.
subfiles.summary: War Minister General Sugiyama denied that the general conscription age would be lowered to seventeen, explaining that younger volunteers were exceptional cases. The report describes plans for seventeen-year-old farmer-soldiers to receive agricultural and military training before settlement and eventual service in Manchukuo or North China. It concludes that Japan had not exhausted its reserve manpower and that rumors of broader reductions in age or physical standards were unfounded.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 2815 on the Mobilization Bill
subfiles.about: The sheet records passage of the Mobilization Bill by the Japanese House of Representatives.
subfiles.summary: The note states that the House of Representatives passed the bill without amendment on March 16. It adds that the House of Peers was expected to offer little effective opposition.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2815: Mobilization Bill
subfiles.about: Grew reports the passage of Japan's Mobilization Bill through the House of Representatives.
subfiles.summary: The House of Representatives passed the bill without amendment on March 16 after initially loud political opposition collapsed. The government promised that Diet members would form a majority on an advisory mobilization commission, while the lower house adopted a face-saving resolution urging restraint in rule by ordinance, civil-service reform, and diplomatic renewal. Grew expected little opposition in the House of Peers.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 2849 and the War Office pamphlet
subfiles.about: The memorandum identifies a Tokyo despatch enclosing a condensed translation of a Japanese War Office propaganda pamphlet.
subfiles.summary: The note refers readers to Tokyo Despatch No. 2849 of March 31. It observes that the pamphlet, unlike earlier examples, had attracted little public attention and points to the despatch's second page for a concise summary.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2849: War Office pamphlet commemorating the Battle of Mukden
subfiles.about: Grew forwards a condensed translation of a Japanese War Office pamphlet advocating prolonged war, stronger armaments, and total national mobilization.
subfiles.summary: Grew summarizes the pamphlet as glorifying Japanese spirit, condemning China's National Government and communism, demanding greater military strength, and calling for a totalitarian economic unit embracing Japan, Manchuria, and China. The Japan Advertiser translation presents the China conflict as part of a wider struggle against Soviet, Western, liberal, and capitalist influences and invokes lessons from the Russo-Japanese War. Its five-part program combines strategic expansion, economic pressure on Chiang Kai-shek's government, ideological mobilization, political support for a new Chinese regime, and diplomacy toward foreign powers. The concluding section defines national general mobilization as control of all manpower and resources, reinforced by loyalty, sacrifice, and expanded armaments.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on military activities in Taiwan
subfiles.to: American Embassy in Japan; Department of State files
subfiles.about: The sheet references a report on anti-spy societies and compulsory training of Taiwanese Chinese adults.
subfiles.summary: The referenced despatch reported formation of societies intended to educate Taiwan's public about spies, with suspicious Chinese as their main targets. It also covered compulsory training groups for adult Formosan Chinese.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the National General Mobilization Law
subfiles.about: The memorandum evaluates Tokyo Despatch No. 2871 transmitting the National General Mobilization Law.
subfiles.summary: The note states that the despatch enclosed the full text of the National General Mobilization Law. It judged the text useful for the files but unnecessary for officials to read.
